item.title: Millions removed from India's draft voter rolls viewed as targeting of Muslims
item.description:
Millions removed from India's draft voter rolls viewed as targeting of Muslims

Submitted by Muheet Ul Islam on Fri, 10/23/2026 - 15:54
Over 100 million people have been removed from the voter list, and many are questioning why specific communities are overrepresented
A student activist holds a poster while on a bus after getting detained during a protest demanding the resignation of the nation's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged voter roll irregularities linked to the 'special intensive revision', in New Delhi on 13 October 2026 (Arun Sankar/AFP)
Off

Sameen Ud Din has lived at the same address in Old Delhi for years. He voted in the 2025 Delhi elections. But when the draft voter list for the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, was published this time around, his name was missing.

“It is an irony not to find my name in the SIR list. I did not receive any notice from the Election Commission of India [ECI] when my name was deleted,” Din, a 44-year-old businessman from the Nizam Ud Din area of Old Delhi, told Middle East Eye.

“I am now being asked to fill out Form 6, an application to register as a new voter, which is clearly a false declaration and carries penal consequences,” he added.

Din said he did not know what would happen next and felt pressured to submit the form. India's next general election is in 2029.

But Din is not alone. Muslims in different parts of India have reported similar problems, with countless people finding their names missing from the draft voter lists.

Approximately 133 million names had been flagged for removal from the voter list.

Critics say many eligible voters have been removed, with Muslims and Dalits – Dalits occupy the lowest rung in Hinduism’s caste system – among those mostly affected. 

An investigation from The Wire shows that in West Bengal, out of 2.75 million on the published list of removals, approximately 1.8 million were Muslims - or around 70 percent of the total published "ineligible to vote" list. Muslims make up just 25 percent of that state's electorate.

In some districts, according to The Wire, removals of Muslims made up over 90 percent of the total published removals.

This disparity has also brought protesters onto the streets of New Delhi. At one mid-October protest, India's Congress Party estimated that 250,000 people were present, while tens of thousands have been protesting across the country.

Protests suppressed

The Cockroach Janta Party, or CJP, called for demonstrations against the SIR under the slogan “Lehra Do Tiranga” or “Wave the Tricolour”. Protesters carrying national flags gathered at Connaught Place before moving towards Dilli Haat and other parts of central Delhi.

“Gyanesh Kumar, resign”, “Down with Delhi Police”, and “Whenever Modi is scared, he sends the police to the front” were among the other slogans protesters shouted.

'Our demand is clear: roll back the SIR because it is a state tool to change the country’s voting demographics'

- Vishnu, protester

The CJP began in May 2026 as a satirical online movement founded by digital strategist Abhijeet Dipke.

At the time, the movement was demanding the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan, a senior leader of the Bharatiya Janata Party or BJP, and the education minister in Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s cabinet. The protest came after the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET), one of the world’s largest medical entrance exams, was leaked; it determines admissions into five-year undergraduate medical courses in India.

It has since developed into a street protest movement.

Today protesters now want the government to stop the SIR and demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

Figures cited by the ruling BJP show that about 130 million names were dropped from draft voter lists during the revision of the list. The ECI says the deletions are meant to clean up the rolls by removing the names of dead, duplicate or ineligible voters.

The protests against these actions took place despite a ban imposed by the BJP-led Delhi government on gatherings of four or more people in some areas. 

The restrictions came after Delhi Police removed Jantar Mantar, an 18th-century observatory and a long-time protest site, from its list of approved protest locations on 12 October. Police named Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground and CBD Ground in East Delhi as alternative locations.

“We are out to protest to protect democracy. There is no violence going on, but the police are still detaining people. It is illegal. These detentions are a symbol of a fascist state, and this has been happening in India for a long time,” a protester who gave only his first name, Vishnu, told MEE.

He was speaking from a private vehicle hired by Delhi Police to transport detained protesters.

“Our demand is clear: roll back the SIR because it is a state tool to change the country’s voting demographics. They have done it successfully in many places, and we want people to join us and fight this fascist government with us,” he added.

Police detained several CJP leaders and protesters during the demonstrations, including Dipke and All India Students Association president, Neha Bora.

Bora was released on Saturday morning. Dipke appeared before a Special Executive Magistrate court and was released after signing a bond, according to reports. Delhi Police registered at least two cases over the march for violating prohibitory orders.

‘Deleted votes are those of Muslims’ 

On 23 September, The Indian Express published an investigation into alleged irregularities at the Election Commission. The report said the ECI had bypassed legal requirements, raised concerns over the SIR and centralised the voter database.

It also reported that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally objected at least 14 times in 10 months to decisions and orders issued without their knowledge, approval or consultation. Their concerns included the addition and deletion of voters, changes to Form 6, access to the electoral database, and the commission’s technology systems.

The ECI rejected claims of an internal rift. It said the notes were suggestions and that every decision taken in the past year, including those related to the SIR, was unanimous. 

Where do Muslim youths fit in India's 'Cockroach' protests?
Read More »

For SIR critics, however, the concern goes beyond the Election Commission's functioning. They say the revisions could determine who can vote and, in turn, affect India’s political landscape. 

Ajay Gudavarthy, an associate professor at the Centre for Political Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University in New Delhi, said available data on voter deletions suggested that Muslims made up a large share of those removed from the rolls. 

He said he believed the deletions were part of a wider political strategy targeting Muslims and Dalits while building support among Other Backward Class, or OBCs, and upper castes. OBC is an official term employed by the government of India and is an umbrella classification for communities that are deprived or disadvantaged, whether economically, socially or in terms of education. 

“An overwhelming majority of the deleted votes are those of Muslims. This is one reason there is no mass outrage against the SIR. The BJP’s larger design is not only to delete Muslim votes but also to socially polarise people on the basis of these deletions,” Gudavarthy told MEE.

“Alongside Muslims, Dalit votes are also being deleted in order to achieve a reverse consolidation of OBCs and the upper castes,” he added.

The experience of Sayed Rashad Ikmal’s family in Odisha shows how the deletion of names can affect voters at the local level.

Ikmal, a resident of Sungra village in Cuttack district, said the names of his aunt and her husband were missing from the draft SIR voter list, even though his uncle had worked in the finance department of Indian Railways.

“The omission came as a shock to the family, which, like several others in the village, worried about being left off the voter rolls,” Ikmal told MEE.

The family approached the booth-level officer and found that a Form 7 application had been filed with the ECI seeking the deletion of their names. Form 7 is used to object to the inclusion of a name or request the removal of an existing name from the voter roll.

The family later approached the Block Development Officer [BDO], who cancelled the request and restored both names to the SIR list, Ikmal told MEE.

He said the BDO's role was important because local officials could prevent people from being wrongly removed from voter lists. 

India's 'Cockroach Party' takes aim at Narendra Modi's government after national exam debacle
Read More »

“If the BDO does his job honestly, wrongful additions to or deletions from the voter rolls can be stopped, whatever happens at the higher level,” he said.

The residents of Sungra and nearby villages, Ikmal said, had begun to feel that Muslims were being targeted in Odisha. He said these concerns had grown alongside the spread of the “Go to Bangladesh” narrative among people linked to Hindu right-wing groups.

“I describe the threat of being sent to Bangladesh as one of the most intimidating narratives directed at Muslims,” Ikmal said, referring to political claims about Bangladeshi infiltration into Assam and West Bengal.

“The narrative had been used to divide voters ahead of state elections in both states and to build support for the BJP,” he added.

For Gudavarthy, the issue points to a larger question about the strength of India’s democratic institutions.

“The system needs to be made accountable only through mass protests and institutional decentralisation,” he said. “It is a lesson for Indian democracy that institutions can be so easily subverted when there is executive overreach,” he added.

item.title: 'Generational rage': Young Europeans fight to be heard
item.description:
From blockaded schools in Rome to tent camps in Madrid and street protests in France, young people across Europe are turning their anger on a political class they say is not listening.

Their demands vary, but they are united in wanting to make their often marginalised voices heard, sometimes even with radical methods in the face of heavy-handed policing.

“We are fighting and taking our future in our hands,” said Damiano Fusa, 18, a student at Rome’s Cavour high school, the first to be occupied in a wave of student takeovers that has spread across the Italian capital.

“We’re not represented by anyone,” Fusa told AFP, criticising both Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s hard-right coalition and previous centre-left governments for cutting education funding and ignoring young people’s needs.

Hundreds of thousands of high school and university students have rallied in France, Italy, Spain and other European countries in recent weeks, with some protests descending into violence.

Governments have largely focused on restoring order, with France imposing partial curfews and Italy deploying soldiers, responses protesters say obscure their demands and could make things even worse.

“Politicians are responding in ways that are completely disconnected from reality, completely absurd,” said Luis Marques, a 19-year-old psychology student in Lisbon.

Students are demanding action on soaring rents, more spending on education instead of defence and more job opportunities for young people.

But experts say the unrest reflects a broader sense among many young Europeans that they have been shut out of politics and sidelined.

“These young people do not just feel like they do not have a place in politics, they feel they are not being heard at all,” said Geoffrey Pleyers, president of the International Sociological Association.

Rosario Forlenza, a professor at Rome’s Luiss University, called it a “European generational revolt” rooted in a social and economic crisis “to which politicians cannot give a substantive response”.

“Young people are a minority of the population that is shrinking and so their social, economic, cultural, political and electoral weight is becoming ever more irrelevant,” he said.

‘Inspiring other people’

The anger has been particularly palpable in France and Italy, where fresh demonstrations are planned for Saturday.

“People are very angry, they’ve had enough. Working hard all day and still not being able to fill up their shopping cart,” a 20-year-old student who gave his name as Eddy told AFP at a protest in Bordeaux last weekend.

“Will smashing everything change anything? I think it can be a jolt to wake up the politicians. We don’t know what else to do to make ourselves heard. The ballot box? We don’t believe in it anymore,” he said.

Protest movements across Europe are increasingly drawing inspiration from one another, and even looking to youth-led movements further afield in places like Bangladesh, India and Nepal.

In Italy, one student slogan last week urged protesters to “do as in France”, while shared symbols, including the Jolly Roger pirate flag, have become common across youth rallies.

Marcos Navarro, 22, a laboratory quality-control technician from Madrid, said protesters across Europe were meeting to share tactics.

“They’ve come to ask us: ‘How did you do it? How do you organise yourselves?’ We’ve already exchanged ideas,” said Navarro, who has been camping with hundreds of others in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square since September to protest housing costs and evictions.

Ayla Herrero, a 26-year-old anthropologist helping at the camp’s infirmary, said it was “inspiring for us to know that we’re inspiring other people, that it doesn’t just stay here”.

‘Not acceptable’

Concern about the rise in military spending in Europe following the Russian invasion of Ukraine has also been a rallying point.

Nikos Mavroudis, a 17-year-old high school student in Athens’ Exarchia neighbourhood, said the money could be better spent on his school, where chunks of plaster are falling.

“It’s not acceptable for classrooms to be dangerous,” said Mavroudis, who hopes to become a cook and plans to move elsewhere in Europe to “countries where things are better”.

At Rome’s occupied Morgagni high school, where students have barricaded entrances with desks, protesters pointed to the crumbling infrastructure as evidence of neglect.

An 18-year-old, who did not want to be named, said the media and politicians in Italy were focusing too heavily on looting and vandalism by some protesters.

“It turns hatred against the students who are victims of this system,” he said.

Asked about the violence, Sabrina Brizzola, 24, coordinator of the Italian University Students’ Union, said organisations like hers should “organise and channel this generational rage”.

“We have shared concerns, even if our ways of protesting differ,” she said.

item.title: UPDF opens fire on tourists, law enforcement personnel in Rangamati's Sajek: ISPR
item.description:
Armed members of the United People's Democratic Front (UPDF) opened fire on tourists and law enforcement in the Gangaram Bazaar area of Sajek, Rangamati district, according to the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR).

The ISPR stated in a press release that the UPDF forcibly used local residents as human shields to block roads.

As a result of the blockage on the Sajek-Baghaihat road, about three thousand tourists visiting Sajek were stranded.

The ISPR press release mentioned that while ensuring the safe passage of tourists, the blockaders created obstacles. In this situation, the Bangladesh Army and police jointly took necessary security measures to ensure the tourists' safe transport to Khagrachari.

While removing the stranded tourists, around 10 AM on Thursday, the blockaders erected barriers in the Gangaram Bazaar area, halting the movement of tourist vehicles. At that time, the army and police patrol team initiated discussions with the blockaders to ensure the safe passage of tourists.

However, during the discussions and around 10: 45 AM, the blockaders, incited by the UPDF, suddenly started throwing stones at law enforcement and targeting tourists, as noted in the statement. To bring the situation under control, the law enforcement used baton charges to disperse the blockaders and resumed the movement of tourist vehicles.

According to the ISPR statement, at approximately 11 AM, it was initially learned that armed UPDF members fired about 30-40 rounds at law enforcement and tourists. During this time, the army patrol team, in self-defense and to ensure the safety of tourists, returned fire, causing the armed individuals to flee the scene. Subsequently, with coordinated efforts by the Bangladesh Army and police, the trapped tourists were evacuated safely, and no casualties were reported.

Preliminary information suggests that the blockade and violence instigated by the UPDF were premeditated. The allegations that locals were coerced into participating in the blockade and being used as human shields are extremely concerning, as mentioned in the statement. It was stated that, due to ongoing security operations in various parts of the Chittagong Hill Tracts, a faction of UPDF's armed members has taken position in the tourist area.

The statement noted that such violent activities disrupt peace, stability, and public safety in the Chittagong Hill Tracts, and adversely affect the tourism industry and the livelihoods of local people. Especially alarming are incidents endangering the safety of innocent tourists and forcibly involving the general public in the blockade program.

The Bangladesh Army continues its efforts in coordination with the civil administration and other law enforcement agencies to maintain peace, harmony, and stability in the Chittagong Hill Tracts and to ensure the safety of the lives and property of local residents and tourists. ISPR informed that the Bangladesh Army will continue its efforts to maintain the peaceful environment of the hill region in the future.

Notably, yesterday, Wednesday, the Sajek Jan Adhikar Raksha Committee and Sajek Karbari Association announced a blockade for the third time on the Sajek tourism road. According to a statement from the organisations, the blockade would continue indefinitely starting today. Therefore, tourists were requested to leave Sajek by yesterday, Wedenday.

Following the blockade call by these regional organisations, the district administration announced the closure of Sajek for safety reasons.

In a public notice last evening, Rangamati Deputy Commissioner Nazma Ashrafi stated that the Sajek Valley tourist center in Baghaichhari Upazila would remain temporarily closed until further notice.

item.title: Dhaka-Chittagong rail services resume after 24 hours
item.description:
Train services on the Dhaka-bound line of the Dhaka-Chittagong route resumed at 12:50pm on Thursday, more than 24 hours after the Karnaphuli Commuter Express derailed in Comilla's Laksam.
The Bijoy Express, travelling from Chittagong to Mymensingh, was the first train to cross the accident site after the line reopened.
Omar Faruk Bhuiyan, station master of Laksam Railway Junction, said train services were now operating normally on both lines.
The damaged track was repaired by 7am on Thursday, but services remained suspended on the Dhaka-bound line because a derailed coach was found. During the suspension, trains in both directions used the other line, causing some disruption. The Chattala Express, bound for Dhaka, and the Paharika Express, bound for Sylhet, passed through Laksam at 10:23am and 10:48am, respectively, on Thursday.
The accident occurred around 12:30pm on Wednesday in the outer section of Naoti station, near Azgara Bazar in Laksam, when five coaches of the Karnaphuli Commuter Express and three wheels of its engine derailed. At least seven passengers were injured.
A rescue train from Chittagong reached the site on Wednesday evening. Recovery work was completed around 5am on Thursday, followed by track repairs.
Meanwhile, railway authorities suspended sub-assistant engineer Sarwar Alam over allegations that he failed to inform the control room about repair work underway at the accident site. He was responsible for the Feni region under the Eastern Railway’s engineering department.
A four-member committee has been formed to investigate the accident, Chittagong Divisional Railway Manager Mostafizur Rahman Bhuiyan said on Wednesday night.

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 1,207 as two die in 24 hours
item.description:
Two more children have died from measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours leading up to 8:00am on Thursday, raising the overall death toll from the ongoing outbreak to 1,207.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified both of the latest casualties as suspected.
With the latest figures, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 1,103, while the number of confirmed deaths remained unchanged at 104, as no new confirmed measles deaths were reported in the last 24 hours.
Among the two new suspected fatalities, both were recorded in Dhaka.
A total of 995 suspected measles cases were recorded in the 24 hours till Thursday morning, taking the overall suspected case tally to 217,760.
During the same period, 36 new confirmed measles cases were reported, bringing the total number of confirmed infections to 23,248.
Since March 15, 2026, a total of 193,608 suspected measles patients have been hospitalized across the country, of whom 185,927 have recovered and been discharged from hospitals, according to the DGHS.

item.title: 4,157 killed in nine months as nation marks Road Safety Day
item.description:
Twelve people died in a head-on collision in Natore on Tuesday. According to police and surviving passengers, the bus was being driven by its supervisor while the regular driver slept in the back.
Two days later, Bangladesh is observing National Road Safety Day with the familiar program of seminars, discussions and promises to make its roads safer.
The latest figures offer little reason for reassurance.
At least 4,157 people were killed and 5,391 injured in 4,285 road crashes between January and September this year, according to the Bangladesh Road Transport Authority (BRTA). That is an average of more than 15 deaths every day.
This year’s observance, under the theme “Safe Roads, Prosperous Nation, Bangladesh First,” comes amid persistent concerns over unfit vehicles, unqualified drivers and the failure to enforce existing traffic laws.
The Natore crash brought several of those concerns into sharp focus.
Police and injured passengers said the RP Special Paribahan bus was heading towards Bonpara when its supervisor, Sohel Rana, took over the wheel after a stop at Ishwardi around 3am.
Ramjan Ali, a surviving passenger from Chapainawabganj, said the regular driver left his seat after the break. About an hour later, the bus collided with a truck, killing 12 people and injuring at least 25.
The circumstances of the crash have once again raised questions about who is allowed to drive passenger buses and how effectively transport operators are monitored.
The deaths in Natore are part of a much larger toll.
According to Bangladesh Jatri Kalyan Samity, at least 125,405 people were killed in 72,736 road crashes between 2013 and 2025. Another 176,249 people were left permanently disabled, the organisation said.
Children have been among the worst affected. Road Safety Foundation figures show that 7,963 children died in road crashes between January 2020 and September 2026.
Nearly 3,000 of them were killed in motorcycle crashes, while 2,812 died as pedestrians.
Yet the problems identified by successive governments and road safety experts remain largely unresolved.
BRTA records indicate that around 650,000 vehicles are operating without the required registration, route permits or fitness certificates. More than 75,000 buses and trucks have exceeded their prescribed economic lifespan.
The shortage of qualified professional drivers for heavy and medium vehicles is estimated at around 30%.
Vehicle fitness is another major concern. Around 70% of buses and minibuses in Dhaka and other major cities reportedly lack valid fitness documents.
Driver health also receives inadequate attention. At a BRTA and Dhaka Ahsania Mission health camp in 2023, around 73% of 541 drivers who underwent eye examinations were found to need glasses.
In 2019, the National Road Safety Council identified seven priority areas and made 111 recommendations to improve road safety.
Experts say there has been little visible progress in implementing them.
BUET Assistant Professor Kazi Md Saifun Newaz said the country already has the Road Transport Act 2018 and Road Transport Rules 2022, but legislation alone cannot prevent crashes.
“Everyone knows the causes of road crashes and their remedies. What is missing is consistent and coordinated action,” he said.
“Observing days will not solve anything.”
The BRTA says it has filed more than 110,000 cases through mobile courts and joint enforcement drives in the first nine months of this year, targeting unfit vehicles, invalid licences, speeding and other violations.
But the continuing death toll raises questions about whether these drives are producing lasting improvements.
Bangladesh Jatri Kalyan Samity Secretary General Mozammel Haque Chowdhury blamed institutional inefficiency, corruption and the influence of transport owners’ and workers’ groups for the persistent disorder.
Road Safety Foundation Executive Director Saidur Rahman said the dangers were particularly acute for children on rural roads, where vehicles frequently pass close to homes and enforcement is weak.
“The authorities know the causes and the consequences, but there is no remedy,” he said.
The government has pledged to enact a comprehensive road safety law by December 2027.
The proposed Road Safety Act 2026 includes free emergency treatment for crash victims, legal protection for people who assist the injured, a demerit-point system for traffic offenders and higher penalties for repeat violations.
Road Transport and Bridges Minister Shaikh Rabiul Alam has also reaffirmed Bangladesh’s commitment to the UN target of halving road deaths and serious injuries by 2030.
For now, the country enters another Road Safety Day with thousands of lives lost, longstanding recommendations awaiting implementation and another deadly crash exposing the dangers on its highways.

item.title: Ukraine and Russia trade strikes following Witkoff talks
item.description:
Russia and Ukraine traded major attacks overnight, authorities from both countries said on Thursday, shortly after US envoy Steve Witkoff held talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg.
Missiles struck Kyiv in the early hours of Thursday, wounding tens of residents, city authorities said.
In an update later in the morning, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had fired 21 missiles towards 12 regions in Ukraine. In Kyiv region, the strikes killed two people and injured 34 others, including five children.
The subway infrastructure on the Southern Bridge over the Dnipro river in Kyiv was also damaged, Mayor ⁠Vitali ​Klitschko ​said ​on Telegram.
“Overnight, Kyiv residents heard what Russian ‘humanism’ truly sounds like: a brutal attack with dozens of ballistic missiles striking energy infrastructure, medical facilities, shopping centers, and residential Areas,” Ukrainian foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on social media.
His post referred to Witkoff recently calling Putin a “humanitarian” for freeing US citizen Stephen Hubbard on Wednesday. Hubbard had been captured by Russian forces and jailed over charges of being a mercenary.
The Ukrainian foreign minister added: “Appeasement, servility, and flattery will not stop this war. Only strength will.”
Another Russian strike killed a woman and injured four others in the Kharkiv region in northeast Ukraine, regional Governor Oleh Syniehubov said on Telegram. A drone also hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure in the Poltava region, local authorities said without providing more details.
Meanwhile, Russia’s Defense Ministry said it downed 808 Ukrainian drones overnight, with many targeting Moscow.
At least two people were killed in the Ukrainian strikes on Russia.
In western Russia’s Lipetsk city, a man was injured as drones hit apartment buildings and a medical facility, Governor Igor Artamonov said on Telegram.
The latest round of strikes came after US special envoy Witkoff held talks with Zelensky in Norway earlier this week, followed by talks with Putin in Russia on Wednesday.
The Trump administration has attempted to mediate between the two sides to end the conflict that began with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Putin agreed “in principle” to resume US-mediated peace talks with Kyiv as soon as next month. Zelensky, too, said on Wednesday that Ukraine supported a US proposal for trilateral talks at the negotiators level to be held as soon as possible.
It was “the closest we’ve been” to ending the war, US President Donald Trump claimed after Witkoff’s meeting with Putin. However, that did not stop the neighboring nations from keeping up a barrage of attacks.
“Almost immediately after another round of talks, Russia launched a pointed attack. This means there has been no real change in its attitude toward everything that is happening,” Zelensky said in a post on social media on Thursday.
“It is important to keep trying to find the right solutions to end this war. But when Russia responds to negotiations with ballistic missiles, real pressure on Russia is needed to bring about different steps – steps toward ending the killing,” he said, once again advocating for stronger air defense capabilities and a faster supply of missiles from allies.

item.description:
At least two people were killed in a strike on a Saudi airport in the eastern city of Dammam on Wednesday, as Washington ordered some diplomats and family members to leave the Gulf country.
Saudi Arabia’s revived war with the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels has intensified in recent weeks, with the Yemeni rebels targeting several major Saudi airports.
The Saudi Civil Aviation Authority said a strike on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam on Wednesday evening killed two people and injured eight others.
The authority added on X that the extent of the material damage to the airport was being assessed.
It did not say who was behind the attack and the Houthis did not claim responsibility.
Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 said flights from the airport were being diverted as operations came to a halt.
Earlier on Wednesday, the Saudi Energy Ministry said forces successfully intercepted a drone targeting an oil facility, but that falling debris killed two people and injured two others. Those killed were identified by the ministry as a Filipino and a Nepali national.
Meanwhile, US State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said his department had issued an order for the departure of non-essential staff and family members at the US embassy in Riyadh.
“Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions,” Pigott wrote on X.
Both Reuters and AFP news agency cited unnamed sources as saying a similar order was also issued for other countries in the Gulf, with the AFP listing the UAE, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain.
Pigott denied the reports, saying they were “inaccurate” and that only employees in Saudi Arabia were ordered to leave.
The US has issued similar evacuation orders on more than one occasion this year amid the Iran war and Iranian strikes on Saudi Arabia in retaliation for the US-Israeli war against Tehran.
A four-year truce between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi rebels collapsed amid the Iran war, with Saudi Arabia experiencing near daily attacks this month.

item.title: Son of Myanmar’s Suu Kyi says had first call in five years
item.description:
The son of Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi said he spoke Thursday to the detained former democratic leader for the first time in more than five years.
“Today, I was finally able to speak with my mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, after more than five years. Hearing her voice again means more than words can express,” Kim Aris said in a post on Facebook.
Suu Kyi is under house arrest in the capital, Naypyidaw, according to Myanmar authorities, where she has been sequestered since being unseated in a 2021 military coup.
AFP could not immediately reach Aris -- who lives in the United Kingdom -- and it was not clear how he spoke to his mother, who won the 1991 Nobel Peace Prize for efforts to bring democracy to Myanmar.
However, he posted images accompanying his Facebook post which appeared to show him standing outside the Myanmar embassy in London.
“I am deeply grateful to everyone who has stood by my mother and me. I believe your voices helped make this moment possible,” Aris wrote.
“But my mother is 81 and remains unjustly detained. One conversation is not regular family access.”
Myanmar’s military held Suu Kyi in almost total seclusion for five years following the February 2021 coup, which ended a tentative decade-long experiment with democracy.
But in recent months authorities have increasingly advertised the loosening of her detention and published photographs of her taking private meetings, as supporters have demanded “proof of life” of the octogenarian.
On Monday, authorities in Myanmar said she received a package from Britain’s King Charles III, including two books about soil and a “sealed diplomatic communication” from the monarch.
Buckingham Palace did not comment on the contents of the communication.
Myanmar authorities said Suu Kyi was moved from a prison in Naypyidaw to house arrest in April, and in August they published images of her meeting the nation’s Red Cross representative.
After ruling Myanmar as military chief for five years, Min Aung Hlaing -- who ousted Suu Kyi in the 2021 coup -- was earlier this year installed as civilian president.
Analysts describe the election putting him in elected office as a charade, and say he may be loosening restrictions on Suu Kyi in a bid to court international legitimacy.

item.title: Bangladesh Bank website shut down to prevent cyberattacks
item.description:
The official website of Bangladesh Bank has been kept offline due to concerns over a possible cyber-attack.

However, internet banking and mobile banking transactions are functioning normally, so customers are not facing any issues with their transactions.

Regarding this, Bangladesh Bank spokesperson Arif Hossain Khan told Prothom Alo on Thursday night that the website is being checked for any faults.

This decision was made due to concerns about worldwide attacks. There are no problems for customers in their transactions as a result.

Currently, the internet and software are extremely important for delivering government services, banking, e-commerce, media, and various online platforms.

A significant portion of these websites relies on the PHP programming language. Recently, after two critical security flaws were identified in PHP, there has been global concern about cyber security.

According to BBC and Reuters reports, after two critical security flaws were found in PHP, a widely used programming language for developing and managing websites, various governments have taken emergency actions.

Following the news of the flaws, governments and commercial enterprises worldwide have shut down their websites since Wednesday night. Despite this, there have been millions of hacking attempts reported.

Using artificial intelligence (AI), a researcher has discovered two highly dangerous flaws in a programming language called PHP.

This programming language has been used in nearly 70 per cent of websites around the world.

BBC's cyber affairs correspondent, Joe Tidy, said that this is an unprecedented situation where IT teams have been scrambling to protect their organisations from a highly serious cyber attack risk, resulting in one website after another going offline.

For example, the Edinburgh Council website, the ''Doctor Who'' section of the BBC website, and websites of various companies in Japan, Belgium, and the Netherlands have been taken offline.

Even some cyber security authorities have taken their own websites offline although they were the ones trying to alert the public about its importance.

As a precaution to avoid potential risks of global cyber attacks, Bangladesh Bank has kept its website offline.

NEIR to curb illegal phones, revenue evasion
item.description:
The Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission (BTRC) plans to relaunch the National Equipment Identity Register (NEIR) in two phases from January 1 to curb annual revenue losses of around Tk2,000 crore caused by illegal mobile phone manufacturing, smuggling and unauthorised sales.
According to BSS, an assessment by the National Board of Revenue (NBR), cited in a working paper presented at a BTRC meeting, found that illegal handsets were causing significant revenue losses for the government.
Under the first phase, the core functions of NEIR will be activated, but handset deregistration will remain suspended. All currently active handsets will be registered automatically, while the IMEI details of unsold handsets held by authorised importers and domestic manufacturers will also be incorporated into the system.
The system will also include provisions to block illegal handsets imported through smuggling or tax evasion.
In the second phase, to be introduced at a later date, the BTRC plans to introduce handset deregistration to verify ownership, detect cloned devices and prevent financial fraud.
NEIR was first launched on a trial basis on July 1, 2021. However, the government later suspended automatic handset blocking and clone-prevention measures.
The NBR renewed efforts to introduce the system on October 29, 2024, followed by the Posts and Telecommunications Division on June 28, 2025.
After directives issued at an inter-ministerial meeting on December 1, 2025, and recommendations from security agencies and inter-ministerial consultations in June and July 2026, a high-level meeting chaired by the home minister on September 22 made the final recommendation to launch NEIR.
Security agencies have warned that unregistered and smuggled handsets are being used in organised crime and mobile financial service fraud, underscoring the need to introduce the system.
Meanwhile, the BTRC has approved a roadmap to phase out handsets that support only 2G networks by December 2029.

item.title: Targeted by Trump, ICC wins top EU rights prize
item.description:
Facing US sanctions, the International Criminal Court was on Thursday awarded the European Union’s top rights prize, in a show of support that risks upsetting President Donald Trump.
“The European Union is built on respect for multilateralism and international institutions, and this prize recognises the important work of the court in upholding international law and justice,” said European Parliament chief Roberta Metsola in announcing the award.
The ICC thanked the European Parliament for giving it the Sakharov Prize “at a time when the Court and its officials face unprecedented challenges”.
“Against this backdrop, the Sakharov Prize carries particular significance, reaffirming the importance of independent judicial institutions and of those who work to uphold international law,” ICC President Tomoko Akane said.
This month, the United States announced sanctions against the ICC aimed at crippling the day-to-day operations of the court, which tries individuals for war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.
Trump’s administration has vowed to dismantle the court “brick by brick”, furious that judges have issued an arrest warrant for Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleged crimes in Gaza.
The win comes after ex-ICC judge Navi Pillay, who also served as UN rights chief, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize this month -- a choice Trump slammed as “disgraceful”, arguing the award should have gone to him.
The EU has already thrown its support behind the ICC in the face of the US sanctions -- which will come into force in six months -- and has said it is “ready to take any necessary measures” to make sure the court can keep working.
“The International Criminal Court must be free to pursue its mission, independently, and without pressure or intimidation,” EU chief Ursula von der Leyen posted online after the prize was announced.
Brussels is hoping to use the delay before the sanctions are applied to try to talk the US down, but is also eyeing implementing a “blocking statute” to shield the ICC from Washington.
Set up in 1988 and named after Soviet dissident Andrei Sakharov, the EU prize is bestowed annually on individuals or organisations to recognise their fight for human rights or democracy.
The ICC was among three finalists this year, alongside Tanzania opposition leader Tundu Lissu and twin sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, representing those prosecuted by the Iranian government.
The nominees are put forward by the political groupings in the EU and the winner is chosen by senior lawmakers. An award ceremony will be held in December.
Lissu, head of Tanzania’s opposition Chadema party, was detained in April 2025. He faces a possible death penalty if convicted of treason for allegedly inciting the public to boycott elections last year.
Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, 21, have respectively been sentenced to death and 36 years in prison for having taken part in anti-government protests in Iran.
Other recent high-profile winners of the Sakharov prize have been Venezuelan opposition chief Maria Corina Machado, deceased Russian Kremlin critic Alexei Navalny and the people of Ukraine.

Of the 5,000 job cuts, 1,000 of the positions have already been eliminated, with another 4,000 layoffs scheduled by the end of this year. Many of those jobs are in developer and support roles.

As Fast Company recently reported, the AI Industry Exposure index, which identifies which industries are most exposed to potential AI disruption—i.e., job loss—found workers in finance and insurance had some of the highest levels of exposure.

“We are positioning Barclays for the future, building the workforce and skills needed to deliver our strategy and meet the evolving needs of our customers and clients,” a Barclays spokesperson told Fast Company in a statement. “This includes investing £150m in our colleagues’ future skills by 2030, with 40,000 colleagues having already accessed our AI learning, which is available to all. For those who may be impacted by these changes, we provide a tailored career support and coaching service.”

The cuts will mainly affect the company’s U.K. retail banking operation, which is heavily staffed in India, where a large number of positions are expected to be eliminated, according to the BBC.

The bank, which is headquartered in the U.K. but operates globally, reported third-quarter earnings on Thursday. For the three-month period ending September 30, it reported pre-tax profits of £2.3 billion ($3 billion), up 12% from the same period last year, but missed analyst expectations of £2.42 billion.

Barclays joins a long list of banks and other companies that have announced layoffs this year in the name of AI efficiency. Those include but are not limited to: Citigroup, which is eliminating up to 20,000 jobs, or 10% of its workforce; HSBC, which reportedly cleared out 10% of its highly-paid senior bankers; and Standard Chartered, which is cutting 7,000 jobs, or 15% of corporate function roles, by 2030.

item.description:
Drops for stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry are dragging markets down worldwide on Thursday, while oil prices hit their highest levels since May on worries about the war with Iran.

The S&P 500 sank 1.3% following even sharper losses in Asia, whose markets are full of AI and other technology stocks. The Nasdaq composite was down 2.4%, as of 12:56 p.m. ET, but stocks outside of tech did better, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down a more modest 40 points, or 0.1%.

AI-related stocks have been shaky on worries that their boom may be under threat because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money to build data centers and buy more AI chips. Concerns also remain that stock prices simply shot too high in their yearslong frenzy, even though companies in the industry continue to report growth.

Lam Research, whose equipment and services help make semiconductors, reported gains in profit and revenue for the summer that were slightly stronger than analysts expected, for example. Usually, that helps boost a stock’s price, but Lam Research’s tumbled 11.1%.

It gave a range for its forecast for profit this quarter whose midpoint was slightly below analysts’ expectations. Its stock also came into the day with a 52.4% surge for the year so far, nearly quadruple the already healthy gain for the overall S&P 500, leaving plenty of room for potential disappointment.

Other big tech stocks were unsettled following their own quarterly reports that included at least some encouraging nuggets.

Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, lost 7.4% after reporting stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, though its profit fell short. The company behind Facebook and Instagram also said it’s creating a new class of stock to raise money to pay for AI investments and other expenses.

Tesla slipped 2.1% after flipping between gains and losses in the morning. It reported a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, though its revenue was weaker than forecast.

The global tide against AI stocks knocked Nvidia down 4.3%. Because it’s the largest stock on Wall Street by total value, the chip giant was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500.

CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy Nvidia’s AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly shaky in recent weeks because of worries about its debt. It dropped 9.6%, though it’s swung between wide gains and losses of roughly 4% within each of the last two days.

The weakness for AI and other tech stocks began in Asia, where South Korea’s Kospi tumbled 3.5%, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 3%, and Japan’s Nikkei 225 sank 2.7%.

Also weighing on global stock markets was a jump in oil prices.

The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 2.9% to $111.99 after touching its highest level in five months. It’s at the high end of the $97 to $112 range it’s been yo-yoing through in October on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal.

In Europe, France’s CAC 40 stock index fell to one of the continent’s sharpest losses with a drop of 1.4%. It has fewer tech stocks than Asian or U.S. indexes, but it was hurt by another jump in yields for French government bonds.

Yields have been generally climbing there because of worries about the government’s big debt load and strained budget. Violent protests across France have raised pressure on the government to increase spending, which could add further to its debt.

Worries about big government debt are weighing on almost every developed economy in the world, including the United States. Such concerns have pushed yields in the U.S. bond market to their highest levels in decades, along with high inflation, signals of a still-strong U.S. economy and other factors.

But U.S. yields nevertheless fell sharply Thursday in a signal that investors were buying U.S. government bonds in search of something safer to own as AI stocks tumbled.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.98% from 5.13% late Wednesday and from more than 5.30% earlier this month. That’s a major move for the bond market, though the 10-year yield remains well above its 3.97% level from before the war with Iran.

Thursday’s drop in yields came even as another report suggested the U.S. economy may be doing better than economists expected. It said fewer U.S. workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which could signal that layoffs remain low across the country.

That solid economy has helped U.S. companies broadly to make bigger profits, which is what propelled the U.S. stock market to a record high earlier this month despite the many worries tugging at it. The majority of stocks within the S&P 500 rose on Thursday, only to get drowned out by the drops for more influential tech stocks.

Procter & Gamble, Lockheed Martin, and CSX were among the latest companies to join the list of those topping profit expectations for the summer, and gains for their stocks helped limit the market’s losses on Thursday.

CEO Shailesh Jejurikar said Procter & Gamble expects “geopolitical and economic challenges” to continue, but it stood by its forecasts for growth in revenue, profit, and other measures for the full year. The stock price for the company behind the Crest, Olay and Oral-B brands rose 6.3%.

—By Stan Choe, AP business writer

AP Business Writer Elaine Kurtenbach contributed to this report.

item.title: The US should stay out of Saudi Arabia’s war
item.description:
After a four year truce, Saudi Arabia and the Houthis have returned to open conflict in Yemen.

Last month, the Saudis conducted over 250 air raids that killed over 150 civilians according to the Yemen Data Project, while the Houthis, officially known as Ansar Allah, relied on drone and missile attacks targeting Saudi oil infrastructure and more recently civilian airports, in attacks that killed 14 people.

A growing Saudi-led coalition to defeat the Houthis is coalescing, but at this point President Donald Trump has resisted requests from Saudi Arabia to resume airstrikes on Yemen, following the truce he concluded with the Houthis in May 2025. That’s not to say the U.S. is staying on the sidelines, of course; Washington has already sent 200 military and intelligence advisors to assist the Saudis.

Mainstream coverage of further U.S. intervention largely misses the critical and concerning context of America joining yet another war against the Houthis: the last Saudi-led coalition war led to one of the worst humanitarian crises in modern history, aggravated by numerous alleged Saudi war crimes. And neither that campaign nor Washington’s recent standoff with the Houthis did much of anything to slow the group’s advances in Yemen.

So why would we join Saudi Arabia in this war — and why do we treat them as a valued ally in the first place?

These are the questions we posed to Quincy Institute Middle East research fellow Annelle Sheline in the latest episode of Always at War.

Sheline has worked closely on Yemen and is intimately familiar with America's human rights record, having worked in the State Department’s Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights and Labor before resigning in March 2024 over America’s blind support for Israel’s war in Gaza.

We asked her about her time at the State Department and why the human rights reports, meant to help enforce rules like the Leahy Law, are so often ignored. What we learned is just how easy it is for these reports to be used to start wars but almost never to end them.

As Sheline put it, human rights reports may be cited as an excuse to hammer U.S. adversaries but are often overlooked or conveniently forgotten when it comes to imposing consequences on U.S. allies, like withholding military support following alleged war crimes. At the same time Annelle’s bureau awarded small pockets of money to journalists or civil society groups working on human rights, the U.S. was sending massive amounts of security assistance to authoritarian governments that kill journalists, like Saudi Arabia.

For Sheline, the math is simple: the U.S. should stay out of Saudi Arabia’s war. The Houthis have repeatedly thwarted U.S. efforts to destroy them, so why try again and risk another disastrous humanitarian crisis? If anything, Sheline believes we ought to push the Saudis toward a negotiated truce, because history has already shown that there is no military solution to Yemen’s profound political crisis.

After all, if America is ever going to end its cycle of permanent war, it’s going to require breaking from the dismal logic of U.S. interventionism that underscored the last decade of Yemen policy — a failing approach that a doddering Joe Biden summarized succinctly late in his term: “Are [US airstrikes] stopping the Houthis? No. Are they gonna continue? Yes.”

item.title: How Long Will Russians Put Up With War? Here’s What They Told Us.
The America-Ukraine link grows even spottier
Technology Is Outrunning the Way We Fight
item.description:
The United States is racing to field AI and autonomous systems. It is not racing to figure out how to fight with them. This imbalance between technology and concepts is widening a gap the U.S. is ill prepared to close. Ukraine has shown us why this gap is a threat: every new capability breeds a countermeasure, and technological advantage now spoils in months. The answer is not just faster innovation. It is making concept development a continuous military function, one that ties new technology to experimentation, validation, and adoption at the speed the fight demands. Not just a function of schoolhouses and Headquarters.

Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022 as a war of armored columns and maneuver. Today, trenches and minefields stretch for hundreds of miles, reminiscent of World War I; while drones, unmanned ground vehicles, precision munitions, and persistent surveillance hunt anything that moves.

The United States has poured considerable energy into buying and fielding new technologies faster, and has shown how we are endeavoring to learn from Ukraine. But the U.S. has put far less energy into the institutional processes we need to determine how we fight as technology and adversary behavior changes. This creates a consequential gap between what we build and how we fight.

This growing gap has two parts. The first is substance: technology and concepts need each other. A concept that ignores new technology will overlook new operational possibilities, while a new technology without a concept is a demonstration… not a warfighting capability.

The second is tempo: technology moves in weeks and months, while the processes that decide how formations should use it operate in years. Our fastest-ever concept cycle, from counterinsurgency doctrine to the Iraq Surge, took eighteen months. Most move slower still: gradual, methodical, and caked in decades of calcified bureaucracy.

The problem isn’t just that doctrine changes more slowly than technology. Units in combat adapt fast. The greater challenge is translating those adaptations into concepts that can be tested, refined, integrated into combined-arms operations, and adopted across the force.

That doesn’t mean rewriting concepts every time a new drone appears. It means recognizing when a change in technology (or in the enemy) breaks assumptions behind how we fight, then testing and spreading the fix before it goes stale.

Concept development must become a continuous military function, not a periodic publication. The winner won’t be the side that buys technology fastest, but the side that turns it into battlefield advantage before the enemy adapts. Today, the U.S. is not built to do that quickly.

Ukraine: Adaptation as Necessity

Ukraine illustrates the increasingly reciprocal nature of battlefield adaptation. To date, every advantage has invited an answer. Both sides have changed their technology and tactics again and again in response to each other, and neither has held an edge for long.

Consider the first-person-view (FPV) drone. Cheap, attritable, and easy to build, FPVs turned every squad into a precision strike force. Electronic jamming became its counterpoint. Fiber-optic drones, immune to jamming, then entered the field. Each move created new openings and new limits, and forced changes in both the technology and how it was used.

The operational consequences extend well beyond FPV drones. Persistent surveillance paired with cheap precision strike has changed where and how formations can move, mass, resupply, and survive. Concealment, dispersion, and deception matter more than ever. A unit that concentrates in a location, moves in the open, or runs a predictable supply route becomes a target.

This is the more consequential lesson from Ukraine: a technological innovation may initially improve the effectiveness of a particular weapon or unit, but its broader significance emerges when it changes the conditions under which formations operate. Then the enemy adapts, and the cycle starts again. And again.

In Ukraine, technological advantage is perishable. The hard part isn’t fielding new capabilities. It’s recognizing when they, or the enemy’s countermeasures, demand a different way of fighting.

The American Challenge: From Innovation to Institutional Learning

For the United States, Ukraine demonstrates why concept development cannot remain an episodic activity conducted in schoolhouses and periodically revisited. The lesson is not that Ukrainian solutions are universally applicable. It’s that new technology and countermeasures can break operational assumptions faster than our institutions are built to respond.

The United States cannot just replicate Ukraine’s approach. U.S. forces fight expeditionary campaigns, integrate across joint and coalition formations, and answer to policy, legal, and safety requirements that a nation like Ukraine, fighting for its survival and territorial integrity, does not. The goal is Ukraine’s capacity to adapt, built to American requirements.

Our gap isn’t a shortage of experiments or innovation offices; efforts like the Army’s “Transformation in Contact” are putting new capabilities into units and learning from them. Our gap is having a pathway from what one unit learns, to what the whole force learns. A concept that works in one brigade may fail against a different enemy, in different terrain, or at a higher echelon. And a successful experiment rarely changes training, force design, or acquisition on its own.

Autonomy has raised the stakes and made our pathway to institutional learning an even greater necessity. A software update, a retrained model, or a new way of employing a system can change how technology behaves, and can quietly invalidate the conditions under which it was tested and fielded.

That is the problem assured autonomy is meant to solve. Assured autonomy is justified confidence that an autonomous system will do what it is supposed to do. It must therefore account for the whole relationship: the technology, how it is employed, and the environment it operates in. Continuous, evidence-based assessments can tell commanders when a change requires fresh evaluation and where the boundaries of responsible use lie. Built into the adaptation process, assurance can support speed without abandoning safety, reliability, accountability, or established approval authorities.

Building an Adaptive Concept-Development Enterprise

The United States needs a repeatable process that links new technology, operational concepts, experimentation against a thinking enemy, validation, and adoption across the force.

We are suggesting neither a prototype nor a concept paper. It’s a validated, revisable concept of employment, backed by operational evidence: how a formation can fight differently, under what conditions that works, and what it takes to make it happen. Four functions are needed to get us there:

First, connect concept and technology development directly to operational formations.

Operators, technologists, testers, and concept developers should work alongside commanders. Their job goes beyond improving systems or inventing tactics: they should identify which operational assumptions a new capability breaks, and draft concepts to test.

Not every improvement demands a new concept. A better jammer may only need a new tactic; a capability that changes how a brigade moves, masses, or resupplies demands a new way of fighting. The force needs people close enough to the fight to tell the difference.

In Ukraine, operational units have designated innovation officers liaising directly with industry; industry partners provide prototypes, receive feedback on battlefield experimentation and adaptation. Through this relationship, operators, technologists, and testers converge on a specific requirement, and battalion-level Commanders have the authority to acquire the necessary prototypes to integrate into their formations.

Second, establish a persistent cycle of adversarial operational experimentation.

The question isn’t whether the technology works as designed. It’s whether the formation using it accomplishes the mission better against an opponent who adapts. Experiments should also find where a concept fails: what works against one threat may fail against another, and a promising system may impose unacceptable costs elsewhere in the formation.

Combat training centers, experimentation units, and operational formations already provide the foundation. The task is to link them into a persistent learning loop, fed by operational evidence and intelligence.

Ukraine offers a cautionary tale. For nearly three years, intelligence indicated Russia was developing jet-powered Shahed variants, by most accounts ample time to prepare countermeasures. But when Russia began launching these faster one-way attack systems, Ukraine had too few interceptors capable of that speed, and their previous interception tactics were insufficient to stop them. The warning did not sufficiently feed a cycle of experimentation before the threat was fielded. That gap cost lives.

Third, connect operational validation to adaptive fielding.

Today, a system is typically tested, approved, and fielded as a finished product. But in a fight like Ukraine’s, nothing stays finished: software is updated, models are retrained, and units find new ways to employ what they have. Each change can quietly invalidate the evidence behind the original fielding decision. Adaptive fielding treats validation as continuous, asking what has changed and whether the earlier evidence still holds.

For autonomous systems, this is where assured autonomy matters most, and where scrutiny should match the modification. A minor software patch for a drone flying the same mission in the same conditions may need only a quick check. Retraining its targeting model, sending it into a new environment, or reducing human supervision demands full re-evaluation. This doesn’t bypass approval authorities or testing requirements. It gives them a faster, evidence-based way to decide when more evaluation is needed.

Fourth, institutionalize validated concepts across the force.

This is the decisive step. Experimentation produces evidence; learning happens only when that evidence changes how the force trains, organizes, equips, and fights.

A counter-drone tactic proven in one division should appear in the next combat training center rotation, the next force design update, and the next acquisition…not in an after-action report on a shelf.

This change requires a defined pathway and clear authorities. Commanders, testers, capability developers, and acquisition officials each own different decisions, but those decisions must draw on a common body of operational evidence, with clear decision points for when the evidence is strong enough to act. The result is a continuous cycle: develop, experiment, validate, field, learn, institutionalize, adapt. Then repeat, as the technology and the enemy change.

In Ukraine, Aerorozvidka, a non-governmental organization, plays this role: not a think tank but an empowered change agent -- capturing evidence from the field and shepherding it through commanders, technologists, and acquisition officials until new tech is deployed or new concepts (like deep strike) are fielded.

Operational Advantage Depends on the Capacity to Learn

The United States possesses substantial technological, industrial, and innovative capacity to compete in AI and autonomous warfare. But technological leadership alone will not produce operational advantage. Adapting a system isn’t the same as adapting a force, and a better-performing unit doesn’t change the course of a campaign.

Four questions will dictate our capacity to learn: The technical question is what a system can do. The tactical question is how formations should employ it. The operational question is how it changes the way maneuver, fires, intelligence, protection, sustainment, and command combine to win. The strategic question is whether the institution can answer all three, again and again, faster than the enemy.

The race isn’t to build the best autonomous systems or to field them first. It’s to turn technological change into operational advantage, faster than the enemy can take it away. In the age of AI and autonomy, the force that learns fastest wins.

item.title: Aurangzeb rules out consumption-led growth, says tariff reforms will continue
item.description:
LAHORE: Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb has ruled out pursuing liquidity-fuelled, consumption-led economic growth, saying Pakistan must prioritise sustainable, export-led expansion and continue with tariff reforms to improve the competitiveness of its industries.

The finance minister was speaking at the Lahore University of Management Sciences (Lums) on Saturday at an event organised by the American Business Forum (ABF). ABF President Osman Khalid Waheed, former State Bank governor Raza Baqir and Habib Group Vice Chairman Salman Burni also spoke.

Aurangzeb said Pakistan could not afford to repeat the cycle of import-dependent growth that had previously led to balance-of-payments problems and forced the country to seek support from lenders of last resort.

He said the government was committed to continuing tariff reforms, primarily to reduce the cost of raw materials and intermediate goods for exporters, despite concerns over the timing of the measures.

“We are very clear: no matter how much pressure there is, we are not going to go for liquidity-fuelled, consumption-led growth,” he said, adding that Pakistan needed to avoid another cycle in which a temporary acceleration in economic activity was followed by a balance-of-payments crisis.

Aurangzeb said the government had attempted to provide a direction towards export-led growth in the latest budget through measures including the elimination of super taxes, reductions in tax slabs and financing for exporters at 4.5 per cent.

On tariff reforms, he said the government had protected domestic industries for too long without sunset clauses and that the existing approach could not continue indefinitely.

“We are in year two of the tariff reform, and we are going to continue with that; there is no turning back,” he said.

The finance minister also stressed that economic growth needed to generate employment, pointing to the contrast between Pakistan’s growth trajectory and that of its neighbour, where growth of 7 to 8pc, he argued, had not translated into sufficient job creation.

“That’s why you see people there where they are,” he said, emphasising that the sectors driving growth must also address unemployment.

Global outlook remains uncertain

Reflecting on discussions at international forums in New York, London and the annual meetings of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Bangkok, Aurangzeb said the global economy had remained resilient but faced an uncertain and worrying outlook.

He identified growing differences in economic fortunes between oil-exporting and oil-importing countries, as well as economies benefiting from artificial intelligence, as key themes in discussions on global growth.

Energy shocks and the El Nino weather phenomenon had featured prominently in discussions, he said, warning that their effects were intensifying and contributing to food-security concerns in some parts of the world.

He also highlighted high debt levels, limited fiscal space in some economies and the growing importance of digital infrastructure and labour-market preparedness for artificial intelligence.

As trade fragmentation and geopolitical polarisation intensified, regional corridors and regional blocs were emerging as significant opportunities, he said, adding that these developments could be particularly important for Pakistan.

Twin deficits narrow

The finance czar said Pakistan had made significant progress in reducing its fiscal and external imbalances, with the combined twin deficits falling from 12.5pc of gross domestic product (GDP) to 2.6pc by the end of the last fiscal year.

He said the fiscal deficit had dropped to a 22-year low, while the country had recorded primary surpluses for three consecutive years. The current account deficit narrowed to around 0.1pc of GDP, supported by remittances and IT exports.

Aurangzeb said IT export services had risen from less than $1 billion to $4.6bn and were projected to reach $5.5bn in the current fiscal year. Foreign exchange reserves had improved to over three months of import cover, compared with two weeks during the crisis.

Citing three credit-rating upgrades since April last year, he said a recent Panda bond had attracted an order book twice its size, reflecting investor confidence beyond Pakistan’s current IMF programme, due to end in October next year.

Conflict puts pressure on energy security

He further said that Pakistan had managed immediate energy-supply challenges amid the continuing Middle East conflict, with supplies secured through November and arrangements for winter underway.

He said the government had shifted from blanket subsidies to targeted support, citing the high cost of universal subsidies.

Assuming an average household size of four to five people, the programme had reached an estimated 40 million to 50 million people, he said, adding that energy and gas supplies remained areas requiring attention.

Debt management and access to finance

The minister maintained that government borrowing had placed a disproportionate burden on the banking sector, but domestic debt-management operations had helped reduce debt-servicing costs to Rs6.9 trillion against a budgeted Rs8.2tr in the last fiscal year.

He said external debt payments had declined from $26.5 billion last year to $21.5bn in the current fiscal year and were expected to fall further. New external borrowing was largely aimed at replacing existing obligations, rather than increasing the debt burden.

Aurangzeb also highlighted pension reforms, saying new entrants to the civil bureaucracy had shifted from defined-benefit to defined-contribution schemes, while discussions with the armed forces were ongoing.

Population, investment and inclusive growth

The finance minister said the government has identified climate change and population growth as major challenges for Pakistan, urging measures to reduce the country’s 2.55pc population growth rate.

He cited Bangladesh, Indonesia and Iran as examples, saying all three had reduced their population growth rates to below 1pc over a decade. He stressed women’s education, workforce participation and engagement with religious scholars as key measures.

Aurangzeb said restoring investor confidence required macroeconomic stability and the clearance of around $4 billion in outstanding dividend and profit repatriation obligations.

He also highlighted improving domestic investment, citing 11 initial public offerings last year — a 20-year high — and five in the current year.

The finance minister said harmonising federal and provincial regulatory frameworks was essential to attract investment, as businesses often faced differing requirements at both levels. He stressed that reforms in taxation, energy and financing were necessary to sustain growth, improve export competitiveness and create jobs.
